The parcellation analyses based on boundary
mapping ( Margulies et al., 2007; Cohen et al., 2008;
Biswal et al., 2010; Hirose et al., 2012, 2013, 2016;
Zhang and Li, 2012; Zhang et al., 2012; Wig et al.,
2014b; Laumann et al., 2015; Poldrack et al., 2015;Glasser et al., 2016; Gordon et al., 2016, 2017; Osada
et al., 2017, 2019; Ogawa et al., 2018 ) were applied to
the cerebral cortical surface. Mean gray matter signalwas regressed out, followed by
spatial smoothing (FWHM =
6 mm). Each vertex in the corticalsurface of each subject was usedas a seed to calculate its correla-
tions with all the vertices. Spatial
pattern similarity of the correlationmaps was evaluated using correla-
tion coeﬃcients, and similarity
maps were generated. Spatial gra-dients of the similarity maps were
computed for each seed vertex,
and the gradient maps of individualsubjects were averaged across the
subjects. After spatial smoothing
(FWHM = 6 mm), a two-dimen-sional watershed algorithm wasapplied to the gradient maps, and
the binary watershed maps were
averaged across seed vertices togenerate a boundary probability
map. The watershed algorithm
was again applied to the boundaryprobability map to delineate parcel-
lated regions.
For subsequent analyses, to
avoid non-uniform signal to noiseratio caused by the diﬀerent
number of vertices in the parcels,
we deﬁned regions of interest(ROIs) of 40 vertices closest to
the centroid of each parcel. When
a parcel contained less than 40vertices, the ROI included all the
vertices in the parcel.


Network construction and
centrality calculation
Correlation coeﬃcients of prepro-
cessed time-series of functional
images were calculated as themagnitude values of functional
connectivity between the parcels.
The correlation coeﬃcientsbetween the parcels weretransformed to zvalues using
Fisher transformation and then
normalized to the standard normaldistribution (average = 0 and
standard deviation = 1). Nodes of
the network represented the parcels, and edgesrepresented the connectivity. To deﬁne a binary
undirected network for each subject, a proportional
threshold of 9% was performed on the matrix offunctional connectivity. The threshold was determinedbased on the clustering coeﬃcients such that the
number of clusters (the structure of three nodes that
were all connected with each other via edges) in thenetwork was maximized using a reasonable number of
edges ( Rubinov and Sporns, 2010; van den Heuvel and
Sporns, 2013; Sporns, 2014 ). The binarized matrix was

absence of functional connections. The centrality indexof each parcel was calculated using the adjacency matrix.
We employed the betweenness centrality that
measures the proportion of shortest paths between allnode pairs in the network ( Freeman, 1978; Brandes,
2001 ). We used the Brain Connectivity Toolbox
(Rubinov and Sporns, 2010 ) to deﬁne the network and
calculate the betweenness centrality of each parcel. If
information was conveyed in the network along the short-
est path, a node with high betweenness centrality medi-ates a high proportion of information traﬃc. Such nodesmay control the information passage or may act as a bot-
tleneck of information ﬂow. The betweenness centrality of
node i was calculated as the proportion of shortest pathsbetween nodes j and h that pass through node i.

In total, 377 parcels (192 in left hemisphere and 185 in
right hemisphere) were identiﬁed in the cortical surfaces
(Fig. 2 A). ROIs consisted of 40 vertices closest to the
centroid ( Fig. 2 B). For the 57 parcels that contained
less than 40 vertices, the ROI included all the vertices in
the parcel. The mean number of vertices in one ROI ofa parcel was 38.8 ± 3.7 (mean ± SD).
Centrality index
Correlation between parcels were calculated on the basis
of ROIs in the cortical parcels. The correlation matrix ofboth hemispheres was calculated and was binarized togenerate the adjacency matrix. Fig. 3 shows the
centrality index in the whole brain averaged across the
subjects. Parcels with high central index were observedin the supramarginal gyrus, anterior temporal cortex and
precuneus.


We also calculated the
participation coeﬃcient, which
measures the degree of inter-network interconnections of aregion that acts as a hub to
facilitate inter-network integration
(Rubinov and Sporns, 2010 ). The
participation coeﬃcient in ROI 1
was 0.37 ± 0.20, whereas that in
ROI 2 was 0.41 ± 0.20. The diﬀer-ence in centrality was not signiﬁ-
cant ( t(19) = 0.57, p= 0.58). ROI
1 did not show signiﬁcant correla-tion with the activity ( r= 0.28,
p= 0.23), nor did ROI 2
(r=/C00.24, p= 0.31).
